# Built to Adapt: Dave Gillespie on Lasting Innovation


November 19, 2026[Mahesh Srinivasan VP & GM, Touch & Display](https://www.synaptics.com/company/blog?author=Mahesh%20Srinivasan) Share this article


Dave Gillespie remembers the moment the scale of his work came into focus. “At some point, I walked into a Starbucks and literally everybody there was using a thing that I had built,” he recalls. “They were either using a phone or a laptop.”


Whether they were navigating with a touchpad or interacting with a touchscreen, those customers were using interfaces rooted in the kind of touch technology Dave had helped develop at Synaptics.


“Most engineers will tell you the reason they become an engineer is because they want to have an impact on the world,” he says. At Starbucks, that impact was suddenly visible in the everyday ways people interacted with technology. As a Synaptics Fellow and recently recognized Distinguished Innovator, Dave has spent more than three decades helping define not only what we build, but how we approach difficult engineering problems.


### From a Practical Problem to a Bigger Opportunity


Dave's career at Synaptics began through Carver Mead, his adviser at Caltech and one of the company’s co-founders. While Synaptics was pursuing ultra-low-power chips for neural networks, a more immediate problem emerged in laptop design. Laptop computers needed a pointing device that could fit into increasingly thin designs. A trackball, by definition, could not become flat. Fellow co-founder Federico Faggin saw that Synaptics’ experience in pattern recognition, imaging, and analog design might offer another answer. What began as a side project to solve the “flat trackball” problem helped set Synaptics on a new course in touch sensing.


Dave saw more than a solution for laptops. Touch offered a compact and expressive way for people to interact with increasingly capable devices. As computing became more portable, those interfaces also had to become smaller, more robust and more efficient, without sacrificing the quality of the interaction. The exact devices and applications were impossible to predict, but the direction was clear to Dave: as devices became more intelligent and embedded in everyday life, the way people interacted with them would have to evolve too.


### Seeing the Whole System


Touch sensing may look simple from the outside, but underneath, it is a system exposed to electrical noise, moisture, static discharge, and the physical differences of every device in which it is installed. Solving only one part of the problem is not enough; sensing, processing, and software have to be designed together.


Working with Tim Allen, Synaptics’ first Vice President of Engineering, Dave helped establish an architecture that brought analog sensing, digital processing, firmware, and software together. Tim focused on the analog side, while Dave led much of the digital architecture, processing, and software. Their complementary expertise allowed the team to determine which functions were best handled in analog hardware and which in digital processing, rather than treating the two independently.


That system-level view became one of Dave’s defining principles. By putting as much intelligence as possible into programmable processing and algorithms, the team could respond quickly when a new form of interference or an unexpected customer requirement appeared. Instead of waiting for an entirely new chip, engineers could adapt the system. In a field without stable standards, flexibility was not an extra feature. It was fundamental to making the technology work.


### Innovation Built to Last


Flexibility also shaped an important early decision. Synaptics’ first touch products combined a custom analog chip with a commercially available microcontroller. By the mid-1990s, the team wanted to integrate those capabilities more closely but could not find a commercial processor that fit its needs. Inspired in part by Federico Faggin’s example as a microprocessor pioneer, Dave helped drive the decision to build one themselves.


The decision was ambitious for a small company, but it created an architecture that could continue to evolve across generations of Synaptics touch products. Dave went on to become a named inventor on more than 80 granted patents globally, including early innovations in object-position detection, capacitive touch sensing and user interaction. His work helped shape touch technologies that would ultimately reach billions of devices worldwide.


The same instinct continues to shape how Dave approaches engineering. More recently, he anticipated the potential for neural-network workloads in touch controllers years before any product needed them. Those capabilities are now being put to use. For Dave, long-term engineering is not about predicting every future requirement. It is about building enough flexibility into the architecture to respond when those requirements arrive.


### Making Room for What Comes Next


His forward-looking mindset extended beyond architecture. Dave helped establish teams focused on concept prototyping, giving engineers a place to explore ideas beyond the current roadmap. The intent was simple: ensure room to work on what could come next, alongside what needed to be solved today.


Dave’s own leadership style evolved in a similar way. In the early years, a small team did a little of everything. As the organization grew, Dave increasingly focused on technical and cultural leadership, becoming more deliberate about giving others room to develop their own ideas. Rather than leading every discussion toward a solution, he learned to listen first, let the team work through the problem, and contribute his perspective where it could be most useful.


That approach is consistent with the way Dave describes good engineering: bring deep expertise, respect what other disciplines contribute, and solve the problem at the level of the whole system.


### An Enduring Focus on Human Interaction


The technologies and markets around Synaptics have evolved considerably during Dave’s career, but human interaction remains a consistent point of connection. His work began with the practical challenge of replacing the trackball with a flat pointing solution for laptops and grew into a broader effort to make interaction with technology more natural, adaptable and useful.


That focus continues to matter as Synaptics brings interface and sensing together with compute and connectivity. Dave has[written about that evolution](https://www.synaptics.com/company/blog/named-after-neurons-how-the-pioneers-of-the-touchpad-built-the-nervous-system-for-robots) from Synaptics’ earliest neural-network work through touch sensing and today's Physical AI challenges. The technology may change, but the challenge at the center of Dave’s work remains relevant: creating better ways for people to interact with increasingly capable devices.


### Keeping a Part of your Head in the Clouds


When asked what he would want others to understand about his journey, Dave returned to the same idea: lasting impact requires thinking about how an invention fits into the whole system around it. Engineers need to keep part of their head in the clouds, while staying grounded enough to build something real.


That balance is evident in Dave’s impact on both technical architecture and engineering culture. The systems he helped create reached people at enormous scale. Just as important, his example helped make room for other engineers to question, adapt and lead. More than three decades into his career at Synaptics, both forms of impact continue.

#### Mahesh Srinivasan


Mahesh Srinivasan is VP & GM of the Touch & Display Business Unit at Synaptics, where he leads the company’s global franchise across mobile and automotive markets. In this role, he drives strategy, execution, and customer partnerships with leading OEMs and ecosystem partners. For close to 20 years at Synaptics, Mahesh has held roles spanning engineering, strategy, and applications, helping scale the company’s OLED touch & display products across top-tier OEMs worldwide. Mahesh holds an MBA from Duke University and an M.S. in Computer Science from Wake Forest University.
